statement: After the two central ID generation services (Amazon and Flickr), the next approach is decentralized ID generation: a piece of logic, not a service. Twitter's algorithm for this is called Snowflake.
detail: The teacher first says 'distributed' and corrects himself to 'decentralized'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Decentralized ID generation logic, not service, logic.

statement: Twitter still uses Snowflake, and the teacher considers it one of the best ID generation systems out there.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So Twitter still uses this. One of the best ID generation system out there.

statement: Snowflake is named after real snowflakes: almost every snowflake in the world is unique, no two are exactly the same, and the ID algorithm likewise produces unique IDs.
detail: The teacher says he only recently thought about why it is called Snowflake.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every single snowflake is unique because of which they named this particular algorithm, if I may call it, as Snowflake.
flags: check: "two words back" - two weeks back?

statement: For the curious: Numberphile has a video on why physical snowflakes (not the ID algorithm) are unique.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the Numberphile has a great video on why snowflakes are unique.

statement: Twitter uses Snowflake for its IDs (tweet IDs); the algorithm has also been adopted by Discord and Instagram, both covered later in the lecture.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Snowflake, this algorithm is also adopted by Discord and Instagram.

statement: Snowflake IDs are 64 bits: deliberately kept small.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So Snowflakes are 64 bits

statement: Keeping IDs at 64 bits instead of 128 bits (16 bytes) matters at Twitter scale: with the amount of data ingested and indexed, 128-bit IDs would literally double the space needed; small IDs give storage and compute efficiency at scale.
case_study: Twitter: data ingested and indexed at Twitter scale.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Imagine instead of having 64 bits, you are having 128 bits, which means 16 bytes. You are literally doubling the space that you need.

statement: Snowflake IDs are very similar to MongoDB's ID (ObjectId), but much smaller.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They are very similar to MongoDB's ID, but very small, very nice.

statement: In a Snowflake ID the first (leftmost) 41 bits are the epoch timestamp in milliseconds: time is always on the left side.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: they have first 41 bits as epoch milliseconds, left side, always time.

statement: Because the leftmost 41 bits move forward every millisecond, Snowflake IDs come out almost ordered; this ordering is a nice byproduct that makes pagination very efficient (shown later).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every millisecond this would always move forward, so you almost get ordering in IDs. That's a very nice byproduct.

statement: The next 10 bits of a Snowflake ID are the machine ID: the ID of the server generating the ID, which is Twitter's API server, not the database server.
case_study: Twitter tweet creation: tweet IDs are generated by Snowflake in Twitter's API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Machine IDs is server that is generating this ID, not database server, it's the API server of Twitter.

statement: Tweet creation with Snowflake: the user sends a REST request to one of Twitter's normal API servers; the server does basic validation (tweet ID, user ID, text, tags), generates the tweet ID with Snowflake and stores the tweet in the tweets DB, which is massively partitioned.
case_study: Twitter tweet creation: tweet IDs are generated by Snowflake in Twitter's API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It generates a random tweet ID using Snowflake and it just stores it into this database.

statement: Snowflake is not a service: it is a library inside the API servers, just normal integer bit manipulation.
detail: The teacher first says 'It's not a library', then corrects to 'It's a library'.
case_study: Twitter tweet creation: tweet IDs are generated by Snowflake in Twitter's API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's not a library. It's not a service. It's a library, normal, normal integer, normal bit manipulation.

statement: Because the machine ID has 10 bits, Twitter's tweet service could have at most 2^10 = 1024 API servers; beyond that the machine ID field would overflow.
case_study: Twitter tweet creation: tweet IDs are generated by Snowflake in Twitter's API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the maximum number of API servers that Twitter would have had for tweet service would be at max 2 raise to 10, which is 1024.

statement: The last 12 bits of a Snowflake ID are a per-machine counter: the same static counter discussed at the start of the lecture, incremented every time an ID is generated. Layout: 41 bits epoch ms | 10 bits machine ID | 12 bits per-machine counter.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 12 bit for per machine counter, that static counter that we discussed at the first.

statement: To generate a Snowflake ID on demand in the business logic the server needs only the current time (it has it), its own machine ID (every machine gets a unique ID to start with) and its per-machine counter.
detail: The machine-ID range is heard as "in range of 0 to 1, 0 to 1, pick one".
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every machine will get a unique ID to start with.
flags: check: "It would be in range of 0 to 1, 0 to 1, pick one" as heard

statement: With a 12-bit counter, one machine can generate 2^12 = 4096 unique IDs per millisecond without any collision.
detail: The teacher first says '12 bytes' and corrects himself to 12 bits; 2^10 = 1024, 2048, 4096.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in 1 millisecond, one machine can generate 2 raised to 12 unique IDs before seeing any collision.

statement: 4096 IDs per millisecond per machine is a humongous throughput: Snowflake was made tolerant enough to be well prepared for future scale.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's a humongous throughput that they have made the system tolerant enough

statement: Snowflake would only see a collision if one machine handled more than 4096 requests in one millisecond; the teacher equates more than 4,000 requests per millisecond to 400,000 requests per second and says no one does that, so with at most 1024 machines Twitter is safe at its scale.
detail: The teacher closes with "And they can at max have 10 machines", apparently meaning 2^10 machines.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: more than 4,000 requests per millisecond implies 400,000 requests per second. No one does.
flags: check: "they can at max have 10 machines" as heard - 2^10 machines?

statement: Snowflake can be written in about three lines of code (even one line).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can even write Snowflake in three lines of code.

statement: Snowflake generation is plain bit manipulation: take the current time, the machine ID and the static counter incremented atomically; left-shift the time by 23 bits and combine the parts with bitwise OR.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Left shift by 23 and set a time, and then set bitwise or, and basically create this ID

statement: Snowflake's benefit: no moving component and no central ID service to talk to; a request comes in, the server generates a Snowflake ID, stores the row in the database, done.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: now there is no moving component, there is no need of a central ID service and whatnot to talk to.

statement: This is why Twitter scales: firing tweets is one of the highest-throughput workloads in the world (people tweet heavily during big events), and a central ID service would itself need to be scaled; Twitter avoids that.
case_study: Twitter tweet creation: tweet IDs are generated by Snowflake in Twitter's API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: firing tweets is one of the most high throughput things that the world is handling right now.

statement: Snowflake IDs are roughly sortable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So the beauty of Snowflakes is that they are roughly sortable.

statement: Within the same millisecond, IDs from the machine with the smaller machine ID are smaller and from the larger machine ID are larger, so even within a millisecond the IDs are roughly sortable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Within the same millisecond, assuming that the machine that has lesser ID is smaller, the machine has larger ID is larger

statement: On Twitter, the tweet ID in any tweet's link is an integer: a Snowflake ID whose first 41 bits are the epoch millisecond when the tweet was made.
case_study: Twitter tweet creation: tweet IDs are generated by Snowflake in Twitter's API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: click on any tweet, look at the link, the tweet ID itself is an integer. This is Snowflake that we are talking about.

statement: Because the first 41 bits are a timestamp, given IDs you can tell whether a tweet was made before or after a certain time, which makes pagination super efficient: an interesting byproduct of roughly sortable IDs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you can very clearly tell if this tweet was made before this time or after this time.

statement: Twitter's API documentation is interesting for how it paginates tweets, e.g. listing all tweets made by a particular account (the teacher notes the API is paid now, though he is not sure of its current state).
case_study: Twitter API: paginating the tweets of one account.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you go through Twitter's API documentation, what you will find interesting is the way you can paginate a tweet.

statement: The most common pagination is limit-offset (also called skip-limit): e.g. SELECT * FROM tweets WHERE user_id = ... LIMIT 10 OFFSET 0, then LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10, OFFSET 20, and so on; SQL is just the example, the same holds for every database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Select star from tweets where user ID is this limit 10 offset 0.

statement: Limit-offset pagination is pathetically slow when you paginate deep.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you do limit offset based pagination, it is pathetically slow.

statement: Example: scrolling the tweets of an account with 10,000 tweets is common; the third, fourth and fifth pages are okay, but the sixth is slower, the seventh even slower, and so on as you go deeper.
case_study: Twitter: scrolling a profile's tweets.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Six page would be slower. Seven would be even slower.

statement: Another example: a batch job computing trending topics processes the last one hour of tweets; Twitter produces millions of tweets in an hour, and paginating across those millions of rows with limit-offset would be very slow.
case_study: Twitter: trending-topics batch job.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Processing last one hour tweets, in one hour Twitter produces millions of tweets.

statement: In 2016, bored at Amazon and heavily into MongoDB, the teacher wrote a quick benchmark of pagination strategies in MongoDB (shown on his blog).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I wrote a very quick demo back in 2016. I was getting bored at Amazon, didn't know what to do.

statement: The pagination findings hold for MongoDB, for SQL, and for literally every database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this holds true for MongoDB. This holds true for SQL.

statement: In MongoDB, limit-offset pagination is skip and limit: each next page fires a query that skips some documents and limits the result.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is limit and offset, MongoDB's example, skip and limit.

statement: Why limit-offset is expensive: for LIMIT n OFFSET m the database must evaluate the entire query, find the result set up to the requested point, skip those rows and then pick the requested ones; this is recomputed on every query, so cost grows linearly with depth.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: your database has to evaluate the entire query, literally find the entire result set until the point that you requested

statement: The other way to paginate is ID-limit based pagination, used when you just want to iterate through a table with no advanced filters or WHERE clauses.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: other way to do pagination is ID limit based pagination, where let's say you just want to iterate through a table.

statement: Twitter commonly iterates through all tweets made in the last N minutes (to find trending topics, do recommendations, put tweets into feeds), so it needs very efficient pagination: ID-limit based pagination.
case_study: Twitter: iterating recent tweets for trending topics, recommendations and feeds.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it's very common for them to iterate through all the tweets that made in last N minutes, right?

statement: ID-limit pagination needs comparable IDs: MySQL auto-increment IDs (1, 2, 3...) are comparable, and so are MongoDB IDs, Snowflake IDs and any ID with time on the leftmost side - you can tell which one is larger.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: IDs are comparable in case of MongoDB and Snowflake and anywhere where you see time on the leftmost side.

statement: ID-limit pagination: fetch the first 10 rows, note the last ID, then query where ID is greater than the last ID with limit 10 (db.students.find with ID > last ID, limit 10), and repeat.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: db.students.find where ID is greater than the last ID, limit 10.

statement: ID-limit pagination is very efficient because MongoDB collections and SQL tables are physically stored ordered by primary key.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: they're physically stored order by primary key, this becomes a very efficient operation.

statement: The teacher's benchmark graph: skip-limit (limit-offset, blue line) time grows linearly as pagination goes deeper, while ID-limit stays constant; at small depths there is little difference.
detail: ID-limit cannot use advanced WHERE clauses; the constant time holds only if you don't need them. The teacher says the linear growth holds for every use case.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you don't have to, you can get a constant time performance while doing deep pagination.

statement: A sudden spike in the benchmark graph was a massive disk flush: the teacher's disk started to throttle, and he was happy to have saturated his IO; the underlying trend is still linear.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: My disk started to throttle at that time and I was so happy that I made my disk throttle.

statement: ID-based pagination gives constant performance because it is a property of the database to always keep data ordered by primary key.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because it is a property of database to keep things ordered by primary key. Always, always.

statement: The teacher has a members-only YouTube video on database engineering topics, including why databases choose B+ trees and how they physically store data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I went into how database actually stores, like why database chooses B+ tree to store it

statement: Because the data is stored in a B+ tree ordered by primary key, 'give me 10 from this ID' takes log n to reach that ID and then a sequential scan; so no matter how deep you paginate, the time does not increase.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's always log n to reach to that particular ID and then a sequential scan after that.

statement: Disadvantage of ID-based pagination: you cannot apply complex WHERE clauses; that is acceptable when it fits your use case.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Disadvantaged, you cannot apply a complex where clauses, but it's okay.

statement: Efficient pagination is a side effect of Snowflake or any ID generation logic that puts the timestamp on the leftmost side.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: any ID generation logic where timestamp is on the leftmost side. You will always see that.

statement: Even in MySQL, when you need deep pagination without fancy WHERE clauses, use ID-based pagination for much better performance - but do not replace all iteration logic, because it does not work with complex WHERE clauses.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But this does not mean you go and replace all of your iteration logic

statement: Epoch milliseconds is a timestamp measured from the epoch, 1st January 1970.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: epoch millisecond is basically time stamp from epoch. Epoch is 1st January 1970.

statement: Nothing enforces the 1970 epoch in the first 41 bits: a company that starts in, say, 2011 or 2015 can use a custom epoch, reclaiming the range lost between 1970 and its start and so getting a larger ID range.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: why should I start my time from 1st January 1970? Can I not get a custom epoch?

statement: A custom epoch gives roughly 35 more years of IDs of headroom.
detail: The teacher hesitates on the figure ("20, 30, 30, for 35 years").
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's huge, like 35 years of IDs you will get it, right?

statement: Discord uses exactly the same Snowflake structure as Twitter, but its epoch starts from the first second of 2015, because the company started in 2015.
case_study: Discord: Snowflake with a 2015 custom epoch.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the epoch time starts from first second of 2015, because in 2015 the company started

statement: Sony also uses a Snowflake-based implementation; it is open source on GitHub, and the core Snowflake code is about five lines of bit manipulation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Snowflake is also used by Sony, the TV company Sony.

statement: Snowflake gained traction because of its decentralization: no centralized ID generation service, no moving part, no external service to scale up and out.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this Snowflake get very nice traction because of its decentralization.

statement: Counterintuitively, the first instinct for ID generation is 'I'll write a microservice'; good engineers instead look at the problem and the most efficient solution - not every solution requires building a service.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Whenever you think of ID generation, the first thing comes up, I'll write a microservice that does that. Good engineers never think like that.

statement: Every system and solution is contextual: it depends on the organization's context, the engineers' expertise and support from management.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every system, every solution is contextual.

statement: If you think your solution (e.g. Snowflake) is superior while everyone else proposes a microservice, bring the change with data-driven decisions: show the data and people will adopt it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You need to have, you need to make data driven decisions. If you show the data, why would they not adopt it?

statement: Teacher's opinion: microservices are stupid and an overkill in most cases; don't fall into the trap of building a microservice for every problem.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Microservices are stupid in most cases. In most cases they are stupid, they are an overkill.

statement: Understand the context, build only what you really need, and keep things simple, because simple systems scale.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Keep things simple, because simple systems scale, always simple.

statement: Snowflake is just a library - a few lines of code - so generating an ID needs no network call and no service to build and scale, which makes it very efficient.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You don't even have to make a network call for that.

speaker: teacher
verbatim: I happened to have Prometheus running at that point of time, which was exporting my node metrics into somewhere.

statement: Asked whether ID-based pagination works for NoSQL as well as SQL B+ trees: it depends on the storage engine; it works in MongoDB (a NoSQL database), as the benchmark showed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Depends on the storage engine. MongoDB, it works well.

statement: ID-based pagination benefits any store that gives sequential scanning (the teacher mentions DynamoDB too) and data locality; with a completely decentralized, hash-based layout where data is de-localized you never get this performance benefit.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you have data locality, then you get this benefit.

statement: Understand how your database stores data on disk: knowing database internals lets you make performance optimizations with confidence instead of defaulting to limit-offset like everyone else.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So understand how your database stores your data on the disk, which is why knowing database internals is essential for you to build performances.

statement: Elasticsearch (NoSQL, sharded/partitioned) offers two ways to paginate and puts a hard-coded limit of 10,000 documents on limit-offset pagination; going beyond gives an error telling you to use the cursor API.
detail: The teacher hedges on the parameter name: "I think they call it offset only".
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Elasticsearch puts a limit of 10,000 documents in a limit offset based pagination. You cannot go beyond 10,000.

statement: When iterating through most documents (more than 10,000), a cursor-based approach is better than limit-offset; for small values it does not matter, the cost creeps up as you go deeper.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's better to go for a cursor based approach versus going for a limit offset based approach.

statement: Asked what the counter in Snowflake is: a per-server static counter, atomically incremented every time an ID is generated - which is why the static counter was stressed early in the lecture.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Atomically increment. Every time you generate ID.

statement: Why a custom epoch helps: the current epoch second (e.g. 1676784716; add three zeros for milliseconds) is already a large number; the 41 bits can hold at most 2^41, so starting from 1970 a new company wastes that range and exhausts it sooner, whereas starting from zero at the company's start lets time count up 1, 2, 3... using the whole range.

verbatim: It will get exhausted pretty quickly because now I'm not starting from zero. I'm starting from this one.

verbatim: So they needed ID sortable by time.

speaker: teacher
verbatim: they put first 41 bits at epoch millisecond, but from 1st January 2011.

speaker: teacher
verbatim: Then the next 13 bits is DB shard ID.

speaker: teacher
verbatim: So 13 for DB shard ID and 10 is per shard sequence number, static counter, right?

speaker: teacher

statement: The teacher's YouTube video on sharding and partitioning was shared in the readings; watch it if you have not.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I hope you saw that video on sharding and partitioning that I put on my YouTube and shared in the readings.

speaker: teacher
verbatim: Instagram uses Postgres as a database, right?

statement: Instagram created many logical shards (also called partitions) on fewer physical DB servers. A physical DB server is the actual server your database runs on (e.g. a MySQL server you spin up); a database created inside it with CREATE DATABASE is a logical partition.
case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Within the MySQL server, you create database by firing create database command. Right. That create database is a logical partition.

statement: Instagram creates thousands of logical shards - at most 2^13 = 8192 - on a few physical servers, e.g. 10 or 15.
case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you create logical shard, which is thousands of them at max 2 raise to 13, which is 8192 at max.

statement: On each physical server you run CREATE DATABASE Instagram 1, Instagram 2, Instagram 3...; another server holds e.g. Instagram 2000, Instagram 5000.
case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: create database Instagram 1, create database Instagram 2, create database Instagram 3.

statement: Every logical partition has exactly the same tables with exactly the same schemas; only the data differs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Database but different data, table same, schema same, data different.

statement: With logical partitions, a migration such as adding a column must be run on every logical database on every physical server - thousands of times (about 8,000).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when you run a migration to add a column, you have to run it on all the databases that you have

statement: Advantage of logical partitions: when a database is hot, a small logical partition can be dumped with SQL dump commands and loaded onto another server, balancing the load.
case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: now they can take a dump of a database and put it into some other database.

statement: Logical partitions and moving them between servers will be covered again in the fifth week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll go into this one more time in the fifth week, right?

statement: With logical partitions, horizontally scaling the database is easy: spin up a new physical server and move a logical partition onto it.
case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They spin up a new physical server, take this logical partition, and move it there.

statement: Without logical partitions, moving data would mean going through every row and extracting the rows to move; separate logical partitions can be dumped and loaded very quickly, making movement easy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: they had to go through every single row and then extract the row that needs to be moved and then move it.

statement: Instagram's structure: about 10 database servers each holding thousands of logical databases; the DB shard ID inside an Instagram ID is the logical partition's ID, at most 2^13 = 8192, followed by the per-shard sequence number.

case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now this database shard ID that here we are talking about is this.

statement: Instagram's brilliant move is using stored procedures (PL/SQL) - something most people neglected in college and assume they will never use.
case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They use stored procedures. Things we neglected in college, PL/SQL, no one studied that.

statement: In each logical database (e.g. insta5) the photos table's ID column is defined as bigint not null with default insta5.next_id(): when a photo is inserted without an ID, the stored function is invoked and its output is used as the ID.
case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when you are inserting a photo in the table, if you don't provide an ID, invoke this function.

statement: Each logical database has its own next_id function with its shard ID hard-coded (e.g. shard_id 5 for insta5), so the stored procedure must be created in every single database.
case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's hard coded there. This is for shard id 5.

statement: insta5.next_id outputs a big-integer result and declares four variables: epoch (the 1st January 2011 epoch millisecond), seq_id, now_ms and shard_id = 5.
case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: First is an epoch variable of type big integer and this is the value which is 1st January 2011 epoch timestamp

statement: Every database has a sequencer - it is how auto-increment IDs are generated: a sequence that atomically increments and returns the next number each time it is invoked.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every database has a sequencer. Like how does database generate auto-increment IDs?

statement: next_id gets seq_id = nextval('insta5.table_id_seq') mod 1024 (2^10): the increment is atomic no matter how many transactions come in, and the mod restricts it to the 10-bit per-shard sequence number.
case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this will be an atomic increment and you do mod mod 1024, so it restricts it to 10 bits as sequence ID.

statement: next_id takes now_ms (the database's current epoch millisecond) and sets result = (now_ms - epoch) << 23, putting the milliseconds since the custom epoch (1st January 2011) into the first 41 bits.
case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now millisecond minus epoch left shift by 23.

statement: next_id then sets result = result | (shard_id << 10), filling the next 13 bits with the shard ID (5), and finally result = result | seq_id.
case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Result equal to result bitwise or shard id left shift 10.

statement: Every insert of a photo without an ID invokes next_id, which generates the Snowflake ID and returns it as the result that gets inserted: Instagram does Snowflake IDs in a database stored procedure.
case_study: Instagram photo IDs: Snowflake-style IDs generated inside the sharded database at insert time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Instagram does Snowflake ID in the database stored procedure.

statement: Implement Instagram's scheme yourself on MySQL, Postgres or any database rather than only studying it theoretically; it is very easy, and the previous batch was amused at how easy it was.

verbatim: Highly, highly, highly recommend you to implement this.

statement: Instagram's approach is efficient because no ID logic is needed on the API side - it is all offloaded to the database; you do a normal insert without an ID and, instead of auto-incrementing, the database invokes the function.

statement: When you create an auto-increment ID column, the database creates a sequence behind the scenes with a unique name; each new ID is a nextval on it. Instagram's scheme replaces that default with a custom-created sequencer - an auto-incrementing sequence that need not be a separate column.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: By default, when you create an ID column with auto increment, it creates a sequence.

statement: A student observed that Instagram just lifted the ID logic from the API server into the DB; the teacher's point: with the logic in the DB there is no limit on API servers - you can have 10,000 or 50,000.
speaker: teacher

statement: Twitter, by contrast, is limited to 2^10 API servers because of the 10-bit machine ID.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Twitter can only have two raised to 10 API servers.

statement: Instagram's limit is instead at most about 8,000 logical databases - a huge number.

speaker: teacher

statement: Snowflake is not monotonically increasing and does not guarantee strict monotonicity; some IDs can be out of order. If you need strict monotonicity, auto-increment is the way to go.
detail: A student asked whether Snowflake guarantees that DB inserts are monotonic for a business case that needs it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Snowflake is not monotonically increasing. It does not guarantee strict monotonic.

statement: A social media app like Instagram does not much care about slight disorder, but a bank listing transactions would not use Snowflake IDs: it needs the strict order in which transactions happened, so auto-increment is the way to go.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Imagine bank, would bank use Snowflake ID? No.

statement: A student suggested that every table has a sequence generated when the table is created.
detail: Corrected by the teacher: that happens only when you have an auto-increment ID column; otherwise you can explicitly create any sequencer with any name.
speaker: student (proposal)

statement: A sequencer's responsibility is to atomically increment: invoking nextval atomically increments it and returns the value.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you invoke nextval, it atomically increments it and returns with the value.

statement: The sequence is created explicitly here because there is no auto-increment column; the name table_id_seq is the name Instagram also gave it, but you can name a sequence anything.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is exactly the name that Instagram also has given.

statement: A table is not limited to one sequence or one auto-increment column: only the ID can be auto-increment is not a hard limit - you can have three auto-increment columns.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can have three columns with auto increments in your table.

statement: The sequencer does exactly what the static counter did in the earlier logic: it atomically increments and hands out values, giving the thread safety needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: which is exactly what a static counter did back in that other logic.

statement: The sequence must be persistent: otherwise, after a database reboot it would start from zero, which is wrong. Leave optimisation (e.g. periodic flushes) to the database; just create a sequencer and let it generate values.

verbatim: it has to be persistent. If not, if not, what if your database reboots? It would start from zero.
